questions.question: How does method chaining work in Ruby?
questions.title: Method Chaining in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Method chaining is calling one method after another on the same result, each returning the receiver (or a new value) so the next method applies: 'hello'.upcase.reverse gives 'OLLEH' (upcase returns a new string, reverse is called on it). It works when each method returns the object the next method needs — strings return strings, arrays return arrays, ActiveRecord relations return relations (where(...).order(...).limit(...)). The chain reads left to right as a pipeline, and it's idiomatic Ruby because most methods return a new value rather than mutating in place (use ! methods like map! to mutate).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand chaining as a left-to-right pipeline where each method returns the value the next needs (strings, arrays, relations).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Chaining a method that returns nil (chain breaks), or expecting mutation from a non-! method.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Chaining calls methods left to right, each returning the value the next needs: 'hello'.upcase.reverse. Works for strings/arrays/relations. Non-! methods return new values; ! methods mutate.

sections.title: A Left-to-Right Pipeline
sections.content: Method chaining is calling one method after another on the same result, each returning the receiver or a new value so the next method applies: 'hello'.upcase.reverse gives 'OLLEH' — upcase returns a new string, and reverse is called on it. It works when each method returns the object the next method needs — strings return strings, arrays return arrays, and ActiveRecord relations return relations, so where(...).order(...).limit(...) composes. The chain reads left to right as a pipeline, and it's idiomatic Ruby because most methods return a new value rather than mutating in place; you use bang methods like map! to mutate the original instead.

sections.title: The Chain Pipeline
sections.content:
Each method returns the value the next method needs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S['hello'] --> U[upcase -> 'HELLO']
  U --> R[reverse -> 'OLLEH']
  R --> D[downcase -> 'olleh']
```

sections.title: Method chaining
sections.content:
```ruby
# Strings return new strings, so they chain:
'hello'.upcase.reverse         # 'OLLEH'
'  hi  '.strip.capitalize      # 'Hi'

# Arrays return new arrays:
[3, 1, 2].sort.uniq.first      # 1
[1, 2, 3].map { |n| n * 2 }.select { |n| n > 2 }   # [4, 6]

# ActiveRecord relations chain (each returns a Relation):
User.where(active: true).order(:name).limit(10)

# The chain breaks if a method returns nil:
'hi'.upcase.reverse.nonexistent  # NoMethodError on nil

# Non-! methods return a NEW value; ! methods mutate the original:
a = [1, 2, 3]
a.map { |n| n * 2 }   # [2, 4, 6] (new array; a unchanged)
a.map! { |n| n * 2 }  # a is now [2, 4, 6] (mutated)
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Chaining a method that returns nil — the next call raises NoMethodError.
Expecting mutation from a non-! method (map returns a new array; a unchanged).
Forgetting that ! methods (map!, sort!) mutate the original in place.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Method chaining calls methods left to right, each returning the value the next needs.
Strings, arrays, and ActiveRecord relations all chain (they return their own type).
Non-! methods (map, sort) return a NEW value; the original is unchanged.
! methods (map!, sort!) mutate the original in place.
If a method returns nil, the chain breaks (next call raises NoMethodError).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Method chaining is calling one method after another on the same result, each returning the receiver or a new value so the next method applies: hello dot upcase dot reverse gives OLLEH — upcase returns a new string, and reverse is called on it. It works when each method returns the object the next method needs — strings return strings, arrays return arrays, and ActiveRecord relations return relations, so where then order then limit composes. The chain reads left to right as a pipeline, and it's idiomatic Ruby because most methods return a new value rather than mutating in place; you use bang methods like map bang to mutate the original instead. A common mistake is chaining a method that returns nil, because the next call raises NoMethodError, and expecting mutation from a non-bang method, because map returns a new array and the original is unchanged.
